blocks.explanation: This is a sum of two squares. With real numbers it cannot be factorized, but with complex numbers it can, because \(i^{2}=-1\) turns a plus into a minus. Plan: write both terms as squares, change the sum into a difference of squares, then use \(A^{2}-B^{2}=(A+B)(A-B)\).
steps:
Step 1: Write both terms as squares
\[4b^{2}=(2b)^{2}\]
\[a^{2}+4b^{2}=a^{2}+(2b)^{2}\]
Why: The difference-of-squares rule needs each term in the form (something)\(^{2}\).

Step 2: Change the plus into a minus with i
\[(2bi)^{2}=4b^{2}i^{2}=-4b^{2}\]
\[a^{2}+(2b)^{2}=a^{2}-(2bi)^{2}\]
Why: Since \(i^{2}=-1\), subtracting \((2bi)^{2}\) is the same as adding \(4b^{2}\). Now we have a difference of squares.

Step 3: Use the difference of squares
\[a^{2}-(2bi)^{2}\]
\[=(a+2bi)(a-2bi)\]
Why: Difference of squares: \(A^{2}-B^{2}=(A+B)(A-B)\). Here \(A=a\), \(B=2bi\).

Check: multiply the factors back
\[(a+2bi)(a-2bi)\]
\[=a^{2}-4b^{2}i^{2}\]
\[=a^{2}+4b^{2}\]
Why: We get the original expression, so the factorization is correct.

blocks.explanation: Again a sum of two squares: \(9a^{2}=(3a)^{2}\) and \(16b^{2}=(4b)^{2}\). Plan: turn \(+(4b)^{2}\) into \(-(4bi)^{2}\) and use the difference of squares.
steps:
Step 1: Write both terms as squares
\[9a^{2}=(3a)^{2}\]
\[16b^{2}=(4b)^{2}\]
Why: \(3^{2}=9\) and \(4^{2}=16\), so each term is a perfect square.

Step 2: Change the plus into a minus
\[(4bi)^{2}=16b^{2}i^{2}=-16b^{2}\]
\[9a^{2}+16b^{2}=(3a)^{2}-(4bi)^{2}\]
Why: Because \(i^{2}=-1\), minus \((4bi)^{2}\) equals plus \(16b^{2}\).

Step 3: Use the difference of squares
\[(3a)^{2}-(4bi)^{2}\]
\[=(3a+4bi)(3a-4bi)\]
Why: Difference of squares: \(A^{2}-B^{2}=(A+B)(A-B)\). Here \(A=3a\), \(B=4bi\).

Check: multiply back
\[(3a+4bi)(3a-4bi)\]
\[=9a^{2}-16b^{2}i^{2}\]
\[=9a^{2}+16b^{2}\]
Why: The product is the given expression.

blocks.explanation: Both terms have the common factor 3. Take it out first; what is left, \(x^{2}+y^{2}\), is a sum of squares, which we factorize with \(i\).
steps:
Step 1: Take out the common factor 3
\[3x^{2}+3y^{2}=3(x^{2}+y^{2})\]
Why: Always take out a common factor first; it makes the bracket simpler.

Step 2: Change the sum into a difference
\[(iy)^{2}=i^{2}y^{2}=-y^{2}\]
\[x^{2}+y^{2}=x^{2}-(iy)^{2}\]
Why: Using \(i^{2}=-1\), \(+y^{2}\) is the same as \(-(iy)^{2}\).

Step 3: Use the difference of squares
\[3\left(x^{2}-(iy)^{2}\right)\]
\[=3(x+iy)(x-iy)\]
Why: Difference of squares: \(A^{2}-B^{2}=(A+B)(A-B)\). Here \(A=x\), \(B=iy\); the 3 stays in front.

Check: multiply back
\[3(x+iy)(x-iy)\]
\[=3(x^{2}-i^{2}y^{2})\]
\[=3x^{2}+3y^{2}\]
Why: We get the given expression.

blocks.explanation: The numbers 144 and 225 share the factor 9 (\(144=9\times16\), \(225=9\times25\)). Take out 9, write the rest as a sum of squares, and factorize it with \(i\).
steps:
Step 1: Take out the common factor 9
\[144x^{2}+225y^{2}\]
\[=9(16x^{2}+25y^{2})\]
Why: 9 is the highest common factor of 144 and 225, so the bracket becomes as small as possible.

Step 3: Use the difference of squares
\[9\left((4x)^{2}-(5yi)^{2}\right)\]
\[=9(4x+5yi)(4x-5yi)\]
Why: Difference of squares: \(A^{2}-B^{2}=(A+B)(A-B)\). Here \(A=4x\), \(B=5yi\).

Check: multiply back
\[9(16x^{2}-25y^{2}i^{2})\]
\[=9(16x^{2}+25y^{2})\]
\[=144x^{2}+225y^{2}\]
Why: The product is the given expression. (The answer key writes the same factors as \(9(4x+i5y)(4x-i5y)\).)

blocks.explanation: A quadratic in \(z\). Compare it with the perfect square \((z-k)^{2}=z^{2}-2kz+k^{2}\): the middle term \(-2iz\) suggests \(k=i\). Plan: complete the square and see whether anything is left over.
steps:
Step 1: Halve the coefficient of z and square it
\[\dfrac{-2i}{2}=-i\]
\[(-i)^{2}=i^{2}=-1\]
Why: In completing the square we always add (half the coefficient of \(z\))\(^{2}\).

Step 2: Notice the constant is already that square
\[z^{2}-2iz-1\]
\[=z^{2}-2iz+(-i)^{2}\]
\[=(z-i)^{2}\]
Why: The constant term \(-1\) is exactly \((-i)^{2}\), so the whole expression is a perfect square with nothing left over.

Check: multiply back
\[(z-i)(z-i)\]
\[=z^{2}-iz-iz+i^{2}\]
\[=z^{2}-2iz-1\]
Why: We get the given expression. The two linear factors are equal (the root \(z=i\) is repeated).

blocks.explanation: A quadratic in \(z\) with no real factors (\(b^{2}-4ac=36-52<0\)). Plan: complete the square, write the leftover positive number as \(-(\ldots i)^{2}\), then use the difference of squares.
steps:
Step 2: Write +4 as minus a square
\[(2i)^{2}=4i^{2}=-4\]
\[(z+3)^{2}+4=(z+3)^{2}-(2i)^{2}\]
Why: Since \((2i)^{2}=-4\), adding 4 is the same as subtracting \((2i)^{2}\).

Step 3: Use the difference of squares
\[(z+3)^{2}-(2i)^{2}\]
\[=(z+3+2i)(z+3-2i)\]
Why: Difference of squares: \(A^{2}-B^{2}=(A+B)(A-B)\). Here \(A=z+3\), \(B=2i\).

Check: multiply back
\[(z+3)^{2}-(2i)^{2}\]
\[=z^{2}+6z+9+4\]
\[=z^{2}+6z+13\]
Why: The product is the given expression.

blocks.explanation: Same type as (vi). Complete the square, write the leftover \(+1\) as \(-i^{2}\), then use the difference of squares.
steps:
Step 1: Complete the square
\[\left(\dfrac{4}{2}\right)^{2}=4\]
\[z^{2}+4z+5=(z^{2}+4z+4)+1\]
\[=(z+2)^{2}+1\]
Why: Half of 4 is 2 and \(2^{2}=4\), so we split 5 as \(4+1\).

Step 3: Use the difference of squares
\[(z+2)^{2}-i^{2}\]
\[=(z+2+i)(z+2-i)\]
Why: Difference of squares: \(A^{2}-B^{2}=(A+B)(A-B)\). Here \(A=z+2\), \(B=i\).

Check: multiply back
\[(z+2)^{2}-i^{2}\]
\[=z^{2}+4z+4+1\]
\[=z^{2}+4z+5\]
Why: The product is the given expression.

blocks.explanation: A quadratic whose leading coefficient is 2. Take the 2 out first so the \(z^{2}\) coefficient is 1, complete the square inside, and keep the 2 in front of the final answer.
steps:
Step 1: Take out the leading coefficient 2
\[2z^{2}-22z+65\]
\[=2\left(z^{2}-11z+\dfrac{65}{2}\right)\]
Why: Completing the square is easiest when the coefficient of \(z^{2}\) is 1.

Step 2: Complete the square inside
\[\left(\dfrac{11}{2}\right)^{2}=\dfrac{121}{4}\]
\[\dfrac{65}{2}=\dfrac{130}{4}=\dfrac{121}{4}+\dfrac{9}{4}\]
\[z^{2}-11z+\dfrac{65}{2}\]
\[=\left(z-\dfrac{11}{2}\right)^{2}+\dfrac{9}{4}\]
Why: Half of \(-11\) is \(-\frac{11}{2}\); its square \(\frac{121}{4}\) completes the square, and \(\frac{9}{4}\) is left over.

Step 3: Write the leftover as minus a square
\[\left(\dfrac{3i}{2}\right)^{2}=\dfrac{9i^{2}}{4}=-\dfrac{9}{4}\]
\[\left(z-\dfrac{11}{2}\right)^{2}-\left(\dfrac{3i}{2}\right)^{2}\]
Why: So \(+\frac{9}{4}=-\left(\frac{3i}{2}\right)^{2}\), which gives a difference of squares.

Step 4: Factorize and put the 2 back
\[\left(z-\dfrac{11}{2}+\dfrac{3i}{2}\right)\left(z-\dfrac{11}{2}-\dfrac{3i}{2}\right)\]
\[=\left(z-\dfrac{11-3i}{2}\right)\left(z-\dfrac{11+3i}{2}\right)\]
\[2z^{2}-22z+65\]
\[=2\left(z-\dfrac{11-3i}{2}\right)\left(z-\dfrac{11+3i}{2}\right)\]
Why: Difference of squares: \(A^{2}-B^{2}=(A+B)(A-B)\). The 2 taken out in Step 1 must stay in front, otherwise the product is only half of the given polynomial.

Check: multiply back
\[\left(z-\dfrac{11}{2}\right)^{2}+\dfrac{9}{4}\]
\[=z^{2}-11z+\dfrac{130}{4}\]
\[2\left(z^{2}-11z+\dfrac{65}{2}\right)=2z^{2}-22z+65\]
Why: Multiplying by 2 gives back the given polynomial.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book labels this part (vii) a second time; here it is part (viii). The answer key (page 297) prints \(\left(z-\frac{11-3i}{2}\right)\left(z-\frac{11+3i}{2}\right)\) without the leading factor 2. That product expands to \(z^{2}-11z+\frac{65}{2}\), only half of the given polynomial. Correct: \(2z^{2}-22z+65=2\left(z-\frac{11-3i}{2}\right)\left(z-\frac{11+3i}{2}\right)\).
